Executive Summary: Advanced encapsulation strategies are essential for extending the lifespan of oxygen and moisture-sensitive devices, such as perovskite solar cells (PSCs).1–6 While traditional glass encapsulations have been the standard, ingress from adhesive joints and protruding metal grids remains a critical shortcoming. In such cases, thin-film encapsulations can address this issue by providing a device-level protection strategy to prolong the operational lifetime of PSCs.7 Additionally, standalone thin-film encapsulations without glass covers play a vital role in advancing perovskite-based technologies as they aim to reduce weight, enhance flexibility, improve heat transfer, and optimize light management.8–15 Moreover, thin-film encapsulations possess an innovative aspect that deserves further exploration: electrical conductivity.16–20 High electrical conductivities, optical transparency, and low permeation rates have been demonstrated using inorganic thin-film encapsulations comprised of metals and metal oxides. These systems can simultaneously function as a transparent conductor and gas diffusion barrier, providing added functionalities across various applications. However, the propensity of inorganic films to form and propagate diffusion pathways, such as pores and pinholes, presents a significant technological hurdle. While the development of effective passivation methods continues to be a significant focus, state-of-the-art polymer- based passivation strategies, particularly inorganic/organic multilayered systems, have yet to be considered due to their electrically insulating nature. In this project, we introduce a novel inorganic/polymer-composite encapsulating electrode comprising an indium zinc oxide (IZO) and a polymer-based transparent conductive composite (TCC).
